title: Sorting Algorithms
blurb: Seven ways to order data, from the O(n²) classics to linear-time counting sort.

algorithms.name: Bubble Sort
algorithms.tagline: Swap neighbours until nothing is out of order.
explanation: Bubble sort walks the array comparing each pair of neighbours and swapping them when they are in the wrong order. After the first pass the largest value has 'bubbled' all the way to the end, so the next pass can stop one position earlier.
It is the slowest of the classic sorts on random data, but it has one nice property: if a pass makes no swaps the array is already sorted, so nearly-sorted input finishes in O(n).
algorithms.example:
Input: [34, 12, 45, 8, 27, 19]
Pass 1 -> [12, 34, 8, 27, 19, 45]  (45 settled)
Pass 2 -> [12, 8, 27, 19, 34, 45]  (34 settled)
Pass 3 -> [8, 12, 19, 27, 34, 45]
Remaining passes make no swaps, so the array is sorted.

frames.note: Start: repeatedly bubble the biggest value to the right.
Index 5 now holds its final value.
Index 4 now holds its final value.
Index 3 now holds its final value.
Index 2 now holds its final value.
Index 1 now holds its final value.

algorithms.name: Selection Sort
algorithms.tagline: Find the smallest remaining value, put it in place.
explanation: Selection sort keeps a sorted prefix on the left. Each pass scans the unsorted suffix for the minimum value and swaps it into the first unsorted slot.
It always performs the same number of comparisons regardless of input, but it makes at most n-1 swaps — useful when writes are expensive (e.g. flash memory).

frames.note: Start: select the minimum of the unsorted suffix each pass.
Prefix up to index 0 is sorted.
Prefix up to index 1 is sorted.
Prefix up to index 2 is sorted.
Prefix up to index 3 is sorted.
Prefix up to index 4 is sorted.

algorithms.name: Insertion Sort
algorithms.tagline: Like sorting playing cards in your hand.
explanation: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix one element at a time. It lifts the next element out, shifts every larger element in the prefix one slot right, then drops the element into the hole.
For small arrays (roughly n < 16) it beats the O(n log n) sorts, which is why real library sorts such as Timsort and introsort switch to it for small partitions.

frames.note: Start: the first element is a sorted list of length 1.
Take 12 and insert it into the sorted prefix.
Take 45 and insert it into the sorted prefix.
Take 8 and insert it into the sorted prefix.
Take 27 and insert it into the sorted prefix.
Take 19 and insert it into the sorted prefix.

algorithms.name: Merge Sort
algorithms.tagline: Split in half, sort each half, merge the two.
explanation: Merge sort is the textbook divide-and-conquer sort. It halves the array until each piece has one element (trivially sorted), then merges pairs of sorted pieces by repeatedly taking the smaller front element.

The log n levels of splitting each cost O(n) to merge, giving a guaranteed O(n log n) — no bad inputs. The price is an O(n) scratch buffer, which is why it is preferred for linked lists and external (on-disk) sorting.

frames.note: Merge sort splits the array until pieces of size 1 remain.
Merge: write 12 at index 0 (from right half).
Merge: write 34 at index 1 (from left half).
Merge: write 12 at index 0 (from left half).
Merge: write 34 at index 1 (from left half).

Merge: write 34 at index 4 (from left half).
Merge: write 45 at index 5 (from left half).

algorithms.name: Quick Sort
algorithms.tagline: Partition around a pivot, recurse on both sides.
explanation: Quick sort picks a pivot and rearranges the array so everything smaller sits left of the pivot and everything larger sits right. The pivot is then in its final position, and the two sides are sorted recursively.

Average case is O(n log n) with excellent cache behaviour, which makes it the fastest general-purpose in-memory sort. A bad pivot choice on already-sorted data degrades to O(n²); randomised or median-of-three pivots avoid that.

frames.note: Quick sort partitions around a pivot (last element here).

Pivot 45 lands at index 5 — final position.
Pivot 27 lands at index 3 — final position.

algorithms.name: Heap Sort
algorithms.tagline: Turn the array into a max-heap, then drain it.
explanation: Heap sort treats the array as a binary heap: the children of index i live at 2i+1 and 2i+2. Building a max-heap costs O(n); after that the root is always the largest remaining value.

Each round swaps the root to the end of the unsorted region, shrinks the heap by one and sifts the new root down. It gives worst-case O(n log n) with no extra memory, but its jumpy memory access makes it slower than quick sort in practice.

frames.note: Heap sort builds a max-heap, then pops the root repeatedly.
Sift down from index 2: compare with its children.
Sift down from index 1: compare with its children.
Sift down from index 4: compare with its children.

algorithms.name: Counting Sort
algorithms.tagline: No comparisons — just tally and replay.
explanation: Counting sort skips comparisons entirely. It counts how many times each value appears, then walks the count table in order and writes each value out that many times.

It is linear in n + k where k is the value range, so it shines for small integer ranges (ages, grades, bytes) and is the building block inside radix sort. It is useless when k is huge, e.g. 64-bit keys.

frames.note: Counting sort works when values sit in a small known range (0..4).

title: Searching Algorithms
blurb: Locate a value fast — scan it, halve it, or hop through it in √n blocks.

algorithms.name: Linear Search
algorithms.tagline: Check each element until you hit the target.
explanation: Linear search simply walks the collection from one end and compares each element with the target. It needs no ordering, no preprocessing and works on linked lists, streams and unsorted arrays alike.
It is the right choice for small collections or when the data changes constantly — sorting first only pays off if you search many times.
algorithms.example:
Array: [3, 8, 12, 19, 27, 34, 45, 52, 63], target 45
check 3, 8, 12, 19, 27, 34 -> no
check 45 -> match at index 6 (7 comparisons)

frames.note: Linear search for 45: check every slot from the left.
a[0] = 3 — not the target, move on.
a[1] = 8 — not the target, move on.
a[2] = 12 — not the target, move on.
a[3] = 19 — not the target, move on.
a[4] = 27 — not the target, move on.
a[5] = 34 — not the target, move on.

algorithms.name: Binary Search
algorithms.tagline: Halve the search space with every comparison.
explanation: Binary search requires sorted data. It looks at the middle element: if it equals the target we are done, if it is too small the answer must be to the right, otherwise to the left. Each step throws away half of the remaining candidates.
A million-element array needs at most 20 comparisons. Watch the mid calculation — use lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1) in languages where lo + hi can overflow.
algorithms.example:
Array: [3, 8, 12, 19, 27, 34, 45, 52, 63], target 45
lo=0 hi=8 mid=4 -> 27 < 45, go right
lo=5 hi=8 mid=6 -> 45 == 45, found at index 6
Only 2 comparisons instead of 7.

frames.note: Binary search for 45 on a sorted array. Search space = whole array.

algorithms.name: Jump Search
algorithms.tagline: Skip ahead in √n blocks, then scan one block.
explanation: Jump search also needs sorted input. It jumps forward in fixed steps of √n until it passes the target, then does a short linear scan inside the block it just skipped.
It sits between linear and binary search. It matters on storage where jumping backwards is expensive (tapes, some paged structures), since it only ever scans forward within one block.
algorithms.example:
Array of 9 items, block = 3, target 45
jump to index 3 (19) -> too small
jump to index 6 (45) -> not smaller, stop
scan block [3..6]: 19, 27, 34, 45 -> found at index 6

frames.note: Jump search: hop in blocks of √n = 3, then scan back linearly.
Overshot the target — the answer must be in block [3..6].
Linear scan inside the block: a[3] = 19.
Linear scan inside the block: a[4] = 27.
Linear scan inside the block: a[5] = 34.

title: Array Techniques
blurb: Pointer pairs, windows and running sums that turn O(n²) loops into single passes.

algorithms.name: Two Pointers
algorithms.tagline: Walk inwards from both ends of a sorted array.
explanation: When an array is sorted, a pair of indices moving towards each other can answer many pair questions in one pass. If the current sum is too small only the left pointer can help, if it is too big only the right pointer can.
The same shape solves container-with-most-water, removing duplicates in place, merging two sorted arrays and partitioning — anywhere a nested loop is doing redundant work on ordered data.
algorithms.example:
Array: [1, 4, 6, 9, 13, 18, 21], target 22
1 + 21 = 22 -> match immediately
If the target were 30: 1+21=22 (small, lo++), 4+21=25, 6+21=27, 9+21=30 -> found.

frames.note: Two pointers on a sorted array, target sum = 22.

algorithms.name: Sliding Window
algorithms.tagline: Reuse the previous window instead of recomputing it.
explanation: A fixed-size window keeps a running aggregate. Moving the window one step right means subtracting the element that leaves and adding the element that enters — constant work per step instead of re-summing k elements.

Variable-size windows follow the same idea: grow the right edge while the window is valid, shrink the left edge when it stops being valid. That solves longest-substring-without-repeats, minimum-window-substring and rate limiting.

frames.note: Filling the first window, running sum = 2.
Filling the first window, running sum = 3.
Window [0..2] sums to 8. Best so far = 8.
Window [1..3] sums to 7. Best so far = 8.
Window [2..4] sums to 9. Best so far = 9.
Window [3..5] sums to 6. Best so far = 9.
Window [4..6] sums to 13. Best so far = 13.

algorithms.name: Kadane's Algorithm
algorithms.tagline: Maximum subarray sum in a single pass.
explanation: At each index you only need one decision: extend the current run, or start a fresh run here. If the running sum has gone negative it can never help a future subarray, so you throw it away.
Keep the best value seen so far alongside the running sum and you get the maximum subarray in O(n) — the classic replacement for the O(n²) brute force over all ranges.

frames.note: Extend the window with -2 — current sum = -2.
Previous run hurts us — restart the window at index 1 (3).
Extend the window with -1 — current sum = 2.
Extend the window with 4 — current sum = 6.
Extend the window with -6 — current sum = 0.
Extend the window with 5 — current sum = 5.
Extend the window with 2 — current sum = 7.
Best contiguous subarray is [1..6] with sum 7.

title: String Algorithms
blurb: Pattern matching from brute force to KMP, plus classic in-place character scans.

algorithms.name: Naive Pattern Search
algorithms.tagline: Try the pattern at every shift.
explanation: The brute-force matcher lines the pattern up at position 0, compares characters until a mismatch, then slides one position right and starts over.
It is easy to get right and fine for short patterns, but repetitive text like 'AAAAAB' makes it re-compare the same characters over and over, hence the O(n·m) worst case.
algorithms.example:
Text "ABABDABACD", pattern "ABAC"
shift 0: ABA matches, D vs C mismatch
shift 1: B vs A mismatch
shift 2: ABA matches, D vs C mismatch
...
shift 5: ABAC matches -> index 5

frames.note: Shift 0: mismatch at text index 3 — restart one position right.
Shift 1: mismatch at text index 1 — restart one position right.
Shift 2: mismatch at text index 4 — restart one position right.
Shift 3: mismatch at text index 3 — restart one position right.
Shift 4: mismatch at text index 4 — restart one position right.

algorithms.name: KMP Pattern Matching
algorithms.tagline: Never re-read a character of the text.
explanation: KMP precomputes the LPS table: for each prefix of the pattern, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. That tells you how far the pattern can shift after a mismatch without missing a match.
Because the text pointer only ever moves forward, the whole search is linear. This is the standard answer for substring search in large streams and the base for Aho-Corasick multi-pattern matching.
algorithms.example:
Pattern "ABAC" -> LPS [0, 0, 1, 0]
Text "ABABDABACD"
match ABA, mismatch at D -> j = lps[2] = 1 (keep the "A")
continue forward, match ABAC at index 5.

frames.note: Prefix table (LPS) for "ABAC" = [0, 0, 1, 0] — how much of the pattern we can reuse after a mismatch.
Now scan the text with a single pointer that never moves backwards.
Mismatch — jump j back to lps[2] = 1 instead of rescanning the text.
Mismatch — jump j back to lps[1] = 0 instead of rescanning the text.
Mismatch with j = 0 — advance the text pointer.

algorithms.name: Palindrome Check
algorithms.tagline: Compare the ends and walk inwards.
explanation: Reversing the string and comparing works but allocates a copy. Two pointers from both ends compare characters in place and bail out at the first mismatch, using constant memory.
The same in-place scan extends to 'palindrome ignoring punctuation and case' and to the expand-around-centre method for the longest palindromic substring.
algorithms.example:
"racecar"
r == r, a == a, c == c, middle e reached -> true
"reactor"
r == r, e vs o mismatch -> false

frames.note: Check a palindrome with two pointers.
Pointers crossed with no mismatch — it is a palindrome.

title: Stacks
blurb: LIFO thinking: bracket matching, monotonic stacks and O(1) minimum tracking.

algorithms.name: Balanced Parentheses
algorithms.tagline: The canonical last-in-first-out problem.
explanation: Every opening bracket is pushed. Every closing bracket must match whatever is on top of the stack — that is exactly the most recently opened, still-unclosed bracket.
If a closer mismatches, or the stack is empty when a closer arrives, or the stack is non-empty at the end, the string is unbalanced. Compilers use the same check while parsing.

frames.note: Closing ']' does not match the top '(' — string is invalid.

algorithms.name: Next Greater Element
algorithms.tagline: A monotonic stack answers all indices in one pass.
explanation: Keep a stack of indices whose answer is still unknown, ordered so their values decrease from bottom to top. When a new value arrives, it is the answer for every stacked index smaller than it — pop them all.
Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total work is linear. The same pattern computes stock spans, daily temperatures and the largest rectangle in a histogram.

frames.note: Next greater element using a monotonic decreasing stack of indices.
Push index 0; it is waiting for a bigger value.
5 is the next greater element for a[0] = 4 — pop and record.
Push index 1; it is waiting for a bigger value.
Push index 2; it is waiting for a bigger value.
25 is the next greater element for a[2] = 2 — pop and record.
25 is the next greater element for a[1] = 5 — pop and record.
Push index 3; it is waiting for a bigger value.
Push index 4; it is waiting for a bigger value.
8 is the next greater element for a[4] = 7 — pop and record.
Push index 5; it is waiting for a bigger value.
Anything left on the stack has no greater element to its right (-1).

algorithms.name: Min Stack
algorithms.tagline: push, pop and getMin all in O(1).
explanation: Scanning for the minimum is O(n), so instead keep a parallel stack whose top always holds the minimum of the current contents. On push you store min(newValue, currentMin); on pop you pop both stacks.
This trades O(n) extra memory for constant-time queries — the standard 'augment the structure with the answer' trick.
algorithms.example:
push 5 -> stack [5],     min [5]
push 3 -> stack [5,3],   min [5,3]
push 7 -> stack [5,3,7], min [5,3,3]
getMin -> 3
pop, pop -> stack [5], min [5]
getMin -> 5

frames.note: push(5) — also push min(5, current min) onto the min stack.
push(3) — also push min(3, current min) onto the min stack.
push(7) — also push min(7, current min) onto the min stack.
getMin() reads the top of the min stack: 3 — O(1).
pop() removes 7; the min stack pops in lockstep.
pop() removes 3; the min stack pops in lockstep.
getMin() reads the top of the min stack: 5 — O(1).

title: Queues
blurb: FIFO structures, ring buffers and the monotonic deque behind sliding-window maxima.

algorithms.name: Queue Operations
algorithms.tagline: First in, first out — enqueue, dequeue, peek.
explanation: A queue serves items in arrival order. Producers append at the rear, consumers take from the front, and neither needs to know about the other — which is why queues underpin schedulers, print spoolers and message brokers.
Careful with JavaScript arrays: shift() is O(n) because it re-indexes. Real implementations use a linked list or a circular buffer to keep dequeue at O(1).
algorithms.example:
enqueue 7 -> [7]
enqueue 3 -> [7, 3]
enqueue 9 -> [7, 3, 9]
dequeue   -> 7, queue [3, 9]
enqueue 5 -> [3, 9, 5]
dequeue   -> 3
peek      -> 9

frames.note: enqueue(7) — new items join at the rear.
enqueue(3) — new items join at the rear.
enqueue(9) — new items join at the rear.
enqueue(5) — new items join at the rear.

algorithms.name: Circular Queue
algorithms.tagline: Fixed buffer, wrap-around indices, zero shifting.
explanation: A circular queue stores items in a fixed array and keeps head and tail indices that wrap with modulo capacity. Nothing is ever shifted, and memory usage is bounded.

It is the structure behind ring buffers in audio pipelines, network drivers and lock-free producer/consumer queues. Track size separately so you can distinguish 'full' from 'empty' when head equals tail.
algorithms.example:
capacity 5
enqueue 1,2,3 -> [1,2,3,·,·] head=0 tail=3
dequeue x2    -> [·,·,3,·,·] head=2
enqueue 4,5,6 -> [6,·,3,4,5] tail wrapped to index 1

frames.note: Circular queue with capacity 5: head and tail wrap around with modulo.
The tail wrapped to the front of the buffer — no shifting, no reallocation.

algorithms.name: Deque: Sliding Window Maximum
algorithms.tagline: A double-ended queue keeps candidates in order.
explanation: A deque allows push/pop at both ends. Here it stores indices whose values decrease from front to back, so the front is always the maximum of the current window.

Two rules maintain it: drop front indices that fell out of the window, and pop back indices whose values are smaller than the incoming value — they are dominated forever. Each index moves twice, giving O(n) instead of O(n·k).

frames.note: Sliding window maximum (k = 3) with a monotonic deque of indices.
a[0] = 1 <= 3 — it can never be a maximum again, pop it.
Index 1 left the window — drop it from the front.
a[3] = -3 <= 5 — it can never be a maximum again, pop it.
a[2] = -1 <= 5 — it can never be a maximum again, pop it.
a[5] = 3 <= 6 — it can never be a maximum again, pop it.
a[4] = 5 <= 6 — it can never be a maximum again, pop it.
a[6] = 6 <= 7 — it can never be a maximum again, pop it.
Every index enters and leaves the deque once — linear time.

title: Linked Lists
blurb: Node chains: traversal, in-place reversal and the tortoise-and-hare cycle trick.

algorithms.name: Traversal & Insertion
algorithms.tagline: Pointer chasing instead of index arithmetic.
explanation: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a reference to the next node. There is no random access: reaching index k costs k hops.
In exchange, splicing a node in or out is O(1) once you hold the previous node — no elements shift. That trade-off is why lists back LRU caches, adjacency lists and allocator free lists.
algorithms.example:
List: 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40
walk: visit 10, 20, 30, 40 (4 hops)
insert 25 after 20:
  newNode.next = node20.next  (30)
  node20.next = newNode
Result: 10 -> 20 -> 25 -> 30 -> 40

frames.note: head points at the first node; each node stores value + next pointer.
Insert 25 after 20: point the new node at 30, then point 20 at the new node — O(1), no shifting.

algorithms.name: Reverse a Linked List
algorithms.tagline: Three pointers, one pass, no extra memory.
explanation: Walk the list once and flip each node's next pointer to face backwards. You need three references: prev (already reversed), curr (the node being flipped) and next (saved before you overwrite curr.next).
Forgetting to save next is the classic bug — you lose the rest of the list. The recursive version reads nicely but costs O(n) stack.
algorithms.example:
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> null
flip 1: null <- 1,  rest 2 -> 3 -> 4
flip 2: null <- 1 <- 2
flip 3: null <- 1 <- 2 <- 3
flip 4: new head = 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1

frames.note: Reverse iteratively with three pointers: prev, curr, next.
Flip node 1's pointer to the previous node. Reversed part: 1.
Flip node 2's pointer to the previous node. Reversed part: 2 -> 1.
Flip node 3's pointer to the previous node. Reversed part: 3 -> 2 -> 1.
Flip node 4's pointer to the previous node. Reversed part: 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1.
curr is null — prev is the new head.

algorithms.name: Floyd's Cycle Detection
algorithms.tagline: Tortoise and hare find a loop in O(1) space.
explanation: Send two pointers through the list: slow advances one node per tick, fast advances two. If the list ends, there is no cycle. If there is a cycle, fast keeps lapping slow inside it and they must eventually land on the same node.
To find where the cycle starts, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time — they meet at the entry node. A hash set also works but costs O(n) memory.
algorithms.example:
A -> B -> C -> D -> E -> back to C
step 1: slow B, fast C
step 2: slow C, fast E
step 3: slow D, fast D  <- meeting point, cycle exists

frames.note: Floyd's cycle detection: slow moves one step, fast moves two.
Step 1: slow at B, fast at C.
Step 2: slow at C, fast at E.
slow and fast met at D — the list contains a cycle.

title: Trees
blurb: Binary search trees and the four traversals every interview asks about.

algorithms.name: In-order Traversal
algorithms.tagline: Left, node, right — sorted output for a BST.
explanation: In-order visits the entire left subtree, then the node itself, then the right subtree. On a binary search tree this emits the keys in ascending order, which is why it backs range queries and 'kth smallest'.
Space is O(h) for the recursion stack — O(log n) on a balanced tree, O(n) on a degenerate one. An explicit stack gives the same result iteratively.

frames.note: in-order depth-first traversal of a BST.

algorithms.name: Pre-order & Post-order
algorithms.tagline: Copy a tree, or delete one, depending on the order.
explanation: Pre-order visits the node before its children — perfect for cloning a tree or serialising it, because a parent is always written before the subtree that depends on it.
Post-order visits children first, so it is the right order for freeing memory, computing subtree sizes or evaluating expression trees where operands must be resolved before the operator.

frames.note: pre-order depth-first traversal of a BST.

algorithms.name: Level-order (BFS) Traversal
algorithms.tagline: Read the tree row by row with a queue.
explanation: Level order pushes the root into a queue, then repeatedly dequeues a node and enqueues its children. Nodes therefore come out grouped by depth.
Memory is proportional to the widest level, which for a complete tree is about n/2. Use it for shortest-path-in-an-unweighted-tree questions, printing a tree, or building a level-by-level UI.

algorithms.name: BST Search & Insert
algorithms.tagline: Ordering invariant turns search into O(height).
explanation: In a binary search tree every key in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every key on the right is larger. Comparing once tells you which half of the remaining tree to discard.

Insertion follows the same path and hangs the new key off the null child where the search fell out. Inserting sorted data degenerates the tree into a list, which is why real code uses AVL or red-black balancing.
algorithms.example:
Search 60 in        50
                 30    70
               20  40 60  80
60 > 50 -> right
60 < 70 -> left
60 == 60 -> found in 3 comparisons instead of 7

frames.note: Search a BST for 60: at each node go left or right, never both.
60 > 50 — go right and discard the other subtree.
60 < 70 — go left and discard the other subtree.

title: Heaps & Priority Queues
blurb: Array-backed binary heaps, sift up/down and the top-k pattern behind streaming leaderboards.

algorithms.name: Heap Insert (Sift Up)
algorithms.tagline: Append at the end, bubble up until the parent wins.
explanation: A binary heap is a complete tree flattened into an array: the children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2, and the parent is floor((i-1)/2). No pointers are needed.
Inserting appends to the end and repeatedly swaps with the parent while the heap property is violated. The tree height is log n, so at most log n swaps happen.

frames.note: A max-heap stored in an array: children of i live at 2i+1 and 2i+2.
Insert 5 at the end (index 0), then bubble it up.
Insert 12 at the end (index 1), then bubble it up.
Child was larger — swap up to index 0.
Insert 3 at the end (index 2), then bubble it up.
Parent is larger — heap property restored.
Insert 18 at the end (index 3), then bubble it up.
Child was larger — swap up to index 1.
Child was larger — swap up to index 0.
Insert 7 at the end (index 4), then bubble it up.
Parent is larger — heap property restored.
Insert 20 at the end (index 5), then bubble it up.
Child was larger — swap up to index 2.
Child was larger — swap up to index 0.
Every insert costs at most log n swaps. The maximum 20 sits at the root.

algorithms.name: Extract Max (Sift Down)
algorithms.tagline: Root out, last in, sink it back into place.
explanation: The maximum always sits at index 0. To remove it, move the last element to the root — which keeps the tree complete — then sift down: swap with the larger child until both children are smaller.
Repeating extract-max until the heap is empty is exactly heapsort, and running it on a priority queue is how schedulers, Dijkstra and A* always pick the next best item.

frames.note: Extract-max removes the root — the largest element.
Take 20, move the last element 3 to the root, then sift it down.
No child is larger — the heap is valid again.
Take 18, move the last element 3 to the root, then sift it down.
No child is larger — the heap is valid again.
Take 12, move the last element 5 to the root, then sift it down.
No child is larger — the heap is valid again.
Take 7, move the last element 3 to the root, then sift it down.
No child is larger — the heap is valid again.
Take 5, move the last element 3 to the root, then sift it down.
No child is larger — the heap is valid again.
Repeated extraction yields the elements in sorted order.

algorithms.name: Top K with a Min-Heap
algorithms.tagline: Stream millions, remember only k.
explanation: To find the k largest values, keep a min-heap of size k. The smallest kept value sits at the root, so any new value only matters if it beats that root.
This is strictly better than sorting when k is small: O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, and it works on streams where the full data set never fits in memory.

frames.note: Keep the 3 largest values using a min-heap of size 3.
8 beats the smallest kept value 2 — replace it.
15 beats the smallest kept value 4 — replace it.
1 <= heap root 8 — it cannot be in the top 3.
7 <= heap root 8 — it cannot be in the top 3.
9 beats the smallest kept value 8 — replace it.
Only 3 items were ever stored — O(n log k) time, O(k) space.

title: Graph Algorithms
blurb: Traversals, weighted shortest paths and dependency ordering on a live graph.

algorithms.name: Breadth-First Search
algorithms.tagline: Shortest hop count in an unweighted graph.
explanation: BFS pushes the start node into a queue and expands nodes in the order they were discovered. Because it finishes every node at distance d before touching distance d+1, the first time it reaches a node is via a shortest path (in edges).

Mark nodes as seen when you enqueue them, not when you dequeue them, otherwise the same node lands in the queue several times. Used for shortest paths in mazes, friend-of-a-friend queries and web crawling.
algorithms.example:
Edges: A->B, A->C, B->D, C->B, C->E, D->F, E->F
queue [A] -> visit A, enqueue B, C
queue [B,C] -> visit B, enqueue D
queue [C,D] -> visit C, enqueue E
order: A, B, C, D, E, F

frames.note: BFS from A explores the graph in rings of increasing distance.
Visit A; enqueue unseen neighbours [B, C].
BFS order: A -> B -> C -> D -> E -> F.

algorithms.name: Depth-First Search
algorithms.tagline: Dive deep, then backtrack.
explanation: DFS commits to one neighbour and keeps going until it runs out of unvisited nodes, then unwinds. Recursion gives you the stack for free; an explicit stack avoids blowing the call stack on deep graphs.
DFS is the base for cycle detection, connected components, topological sorting, bridges and articulation points — anything that cares about the structure of exploration rather than distance.
algorithms.example:
Start A
A -> B -> D -> F (dead end, backtrack)
back to A -> C -> E -> F (seen)
order: A, B, D, F, C, E

frames.note: DFS follows one branch as deep as possible before backtracking.
F has no unvisited neighbours left — backtrack.
D has no unvisited neighbours left — backtrack.
B has no unvisited neighbours left — backtrack.
E has no unvisited neighbours left — backtrack.
C has no unvisited neighbours left — backtrack.
A has no unvisited neighbours left — backtrack.
DFS order: A -> B -> D -> F -> C -> E.

algorithms.name: Dijkstra's Shortest Path
algorithms.tagline: Greedily settle the closest unfinished node.
explanation: Dijkstra keeps a tentative distance for every node. It repeatedly picks the unsettled node with the smallest distance — that value is provably final — and relaxes its outgoing edges, i.e. improves neighbours when going through this node is cheaper.
A binary heap turns the 'pick the smallest' step into O(log V). Negative edge weights break the correctness argument; use Bellman-Ford there.
algorithms.example:
A->B 4, A->C 2, C->B 1, B->D 5, C->E 8, D->F 3, E->F 2
settle A (0) -> B=4, C=2
settle C (2) -> B=3, E=10
settle B (3) -> D=8
settle D (8) -> F=11
settle E (10) -> F stays 11
A to F = 11

frames.note: Dijkstra from A. Every distance starts at infinity except the source.
Settle A — its distance 0 can no longer improve.
Relax A -> B: new best distance 4.
Relax A -> C: new best distance 2.
Settle C — its distance 2 can no longer improve.
Relax C -> B: new best distance 3.
Relax C -> E: new best distance 10.
Settle B — its distance 3 can no longer improve.
Relax B -> D: new best distance 8.
Settle D — its distance 8 can no longer improve.
Relax D -> F: new best distance 11.
Settle E — its distance 10 can no longer improve.
Settle F — its distance 11 can no longer improve.

algorithms.name: Topological Sort (Kahn)
algorithms.tagline: Order tasks so every dependency comes first.
explanation: Count how many incoming edges each node has. Nodes with zero in-degree have no unmet dependencies, so they can be emitted immediately; removing them decrements their neighbours and may free more nodes.
If the queue empties before every node is emitted, the leftovers form a cycle — which is exactly how build systems and package managers detect circular dependencies.
algorithms.example:
in-degrees: A0 B2 C1 D1 E1 F2
emit A -> B1 C0
emit C -> B0 E0
emit B -> D0
emit D, E -> F0
emit F
order: A, C, B, E, D, F

frames.note: Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take a node with in-degree 0.
Output A; decrement its neighbours' in-degrees.
Output C; decrement its neighbours' in-degrees.
Output B; decrement its neighbours' in-degrees.
Output E; decrement its neighbours' in-degrees.
Output D; decrement its neighbours' in-degrees.
Output F; decrement its neighbours' in-degrees.
Topological order: A -> C -> B -> E -> D -> F. If nodes were left over, the graph had a cycle.

title: Tries
blurb: Prefix trees for dictionaries, autocomplete and fast string membership.

algorithms.name: Trie Insert
algorithms.tagline: Words that share a prefix share a path.
explanation: A trie stores strings as paths of single characters from a root. Inserting walks one character at a time, creating a child only when the edge does not already exist, and flags the final node as end-of-word.
Cost depends on the word length L, never on how many words are already stored. Shared prefixes are stored once, which is why tries compress dictionaries and route tables so well.
algorithms.example:
insert "car" -> root-c-a-r
insert "cat" -> reuses c-a, adds t
insert "cap" -> reuses c-a, adds p
insert "dog" -> new branch root-d-o-g

frames.note: A trie starts as a single empty root node.
Insert "cat": 'c' already exists — reuse the shared prefix.
Insert "cat": 'a' already exists — reuse the shared prefix.
Insert "cap": 'c' already exists — reuse the shared prefix.
Insert "cap": 'a' already exists — reuse the shared prefix.
All four words stored; 'car', 'cat' and 'cap' share the prefix 'ca'.

algorithms.name: Trie Search
algorithms.tagline: Exact lookup in O(word length).
explanation: Searching follows one edge per character. A missing edge means the word is absent and you can stop straight away — no hashing of the whole string and no collisions to resolve.
Reaching the last character is not enough: the node must also carry the end-of-word flag, otherwise you only matched a prefix of some longer word.
algorithms.example:
search "cat": c -> a -> t, end flag true -> found
search "ca":  c -> a, end flag false -> not a stored word
search "cab": c -> a, no 'b' edge -> stop, not found

frames.note: Search for "cat" by walking one edge per character.
Node reached and flagged as end-of-word — "cat" exists. Cost is O(length), independent of dictionary size.
Searching "cab" would fail at 'b': there is no such edge, so we stop immediately.

algorithms.name: Prefix Autocomplete
algorithms.tagline: Everything under a node shares its prefix.
explanation: Autocomplete is two phases: walk down to the node for the typed prefix, then depth-first collect every end-of-word node beneath it. Cost is the prefix length plus the number of results.
This is what powers search suggestion boxes, IDE completion and IP prefix routing. Storing a top-k list on each node turns ranked suggestions into a constant-time read.
algorithms.example:
Dictionary: car, cat, cap, dog
prefix "ca" -> node reached after 2 hops
DFS below -> car, cat, cap
prefix "do" -> dog

frames.note: Walk down to the node for 'ca'.
Every leaf under the prefix node is a completion.

title: Hashing & Hash Maps
blurb: Buckets, collisions and the two-sum trick that turns quadratic scans linear.

algorithms.name: Hash Table & Collisions
algorithms.tagline: O(1) average lookups, if the hash behaves.
explanation: A hash function maps a key to a bucket index. Since many keys share a bucket, collisions must be resolved — by chaining (a list per bucket) or by open addressing (probe for the next free slot, as animated here).
Average operations are O(1), but a bad hash or a full table degrades to O(n). Real implementations keep the load factor below ~0.75 and resize by rehashing everything into a larger table.
algorithms.example:
size 7, h(s) = rolling 31-base mod 7
"cat" -> 3   stored at 3
"dog" -> 3   collision -> probe -> 4
"owl" -> 6   stored at 6
lookup "dog": start at 3, probe to 4, found.

frames.note: A table of 7 buckets. hash(key) picks the slot; collisions are resolved by linear probing.
Slot 6 already holds "dog" — collision, probe the next slot.
Lookup "owl" hashes straight to its region and is found in O(1) average time.

algorithms.name: Two Sum with a Map
algorithms.tagline: Trade O(n) memory for an O(n²) -> O(n) win.
explanation: Instead of checking every pair, ask a different question at each element: have I already seen the complement target − x? A hash map answers that in constant time.
This 'remember what you've seen' pattern powers subarray-sum, longest-substring and duplicate-detection problems too. The cost is O(n) extra memory.
algorithms.example:
[2, 7, 11, 15, 3, 6], target 9
i=0 need 7 -> not seen, store 2
i=1 need 2 -> seen at index 0
Answer: indices [0, 1]

frames.note: Find two numbers summing to 9 in one pass using a hash map.
At 2 we need 7. Is it in the map?
Not yet — remember 2 and move on.
At 7 we need 2. Is it in the map?
Yes — 2 was at index 0. Pair found in O(n).

algorithms.name: Frequency Counting
algorithms.tagline: One map, dozens of problems.
explanation: Counting occurrences is the most reused hashing pattern: anagrams, majority element, group-by, top-k and sliding-window character problems all start with a frequency map.
Space is O(k) where k is the number of distinct keys — for lowercase letters that is a fixed 26-slot array, which is faster than a general hash map.
algorithms.example:
"mississippi"
m:1  i:4  s:4  p:2
most frequent: i (4)
Anagram check: two strings match iff their maps are identical.

frames.note: Count character frequencies with a hash map — one pass, O(1) per update.
Most frequent character is 'i' with 4 occurrences — anagram and grouping problems use the same map.

title: Matrix & 2D Grids
blurb: Spiral walks, in-place rotation and flood fill over two-dimensional data.

algorithms.name: Spiral Traversal
algorithms.tagline: Four moving boundaries peel the matrix ring by ring.
explanation: Keep four bounds — top, bottom, left, right. Walk left→right along the top, top→bottom down the right, right→left along the bottom, bottom→top up the left, then shrink each bound inward.
The two guard checks before the bottom and left passes matter: without them a single leftover row or column is emitted twice. Excluding the output list, no extra memory is used.

frames.note: Spiral order: walk the outer ring, shrink the bounds, repeat.
Each cell is visited exactly once — O(rows x cols).

algorithms.name: Rotate 90° In Place
algorithms.tagline: Transpose, then reverse each row.
explanation: A clockwise rotation maps (r, c) to (c, n−1−r). Doing that directly needs a second matrix, but the same mapping factors into two cheap in-place passes.
First transpose — swap every pair across the main diagonal, iterating only the upper triangle so nothing is swapped twice. Then reverse each row. For counter-clockwise, reverse the columns instead.
algorithms.example:
start        transpose      reverse rows
1 2 3        1 4 7          7 4 1
4 5 6   ->   2 5 8    ->    8 5 2
7 8 9        3 6 9          9 6 3

frames.note: Rotate 90° clockwise in place: transpose first, then reverse each row.
Transposed. Now reverse every row to finish the rotation.

algorithms.name: Number of Islands (Flood Fill)
algorithms.tagline: Grid DFS: every unvisited 1 seeds a new component.
explanation: Treat the grid as a graph where each land cell is a node connected to its four neighbours. Scanning the grid and flood-filling from every unvisited land cell counts connected components.

Mark cells as visited when they are pushed, not when they are popped — otherwise the same cell enters the stack many times. Worst-case stack depth is the whole grid, so an explicit stack avoids recursion limits.
algorithms.example:
1 1 0 0 0
1 1 0 0 1
0 0 1 0 1
0 0 0 1 1

island 1: top-left 2x2 block
island 2: single cell (2,2)
island 3: right-hand L shape
answer: 3

frames.note: Count islands: every unvisited 1 starts a flood fill over its 4-connected neighbours.
(1, 0) is land and connected — add it to island #1.
(0, 1) is land and connected — add it to island #1.
(1, 1) is land and connected — add it to island #1.
(2, 4) is land and connected — add it to island #2.
(3, 4) is land and connected — add it to island #2.
(3, 3) is land and connected — add it to island #2.
Each cell is pushed at most once, so the sweep is O(rows x cols).

title: Recursion
blurb: Base cases, call stacks and recursion trees — including why naive Fibonacci is a trap.

algorithms.name: Factorial & the Call Stack
algorithms.tagline: Base case, recursive case, unwinding.
explanation: Every recursive function needs two things: a base case that returns without recursing, and a recursive case that moves strictly towards it. Miss either and you get a stack overflow.

Each pending call occupies a stack frame, so recursion depth is memory. Watch the animation: the stack grows to n frames before a single value is returned, then collapses as results multiply on the way out.

frames.note: fact(5) cannot answer yet — it calls fact(4) first.
fact(4) cannot answer yet — it calls fact(3) first.
fact(3) cannot answer yet — it calls fact(2) first.
fact(2) cannot answer yet — it calls fact(1) first.
fact(1) cannot answer yet — it calls fact(0) first.
fact(1) hits the base case and returns 1 — the recursion stops here.
The stack is empty and fact(5) = 120.

algorithms.name: Recursion Tree (Fibonacci)
algorithms.tagline: Why naive branching recursion explodes.
explanation: Each fib call spawns two more, so the number of calls roughly doubles per level — that is the exponential blow-up you can see in the call tree.
The fix is to notice repeated subproblems: fib(2) is computed twice for n = 4, and thousands of times for n = 30. Caching results (memoisation) turns the tree into a line and the cost into O(n).
algorithms.example:
fib(4)
├─ fib(3)
│  ├─ fib(2) -> fib(1) + fib(0)
│  └─ fib(1)
└─ fib(2)      <- recomputed
9 calls for n = 4; 2.7 million for n = 30.

frames.note: Naive recursion builds a whole call tree for fib(4).
The right branch recomputes fib(2) from scratch — this duplication is why naive fib is exponential.
fib(4) = 3 after 9 calls. Memoising the repeated subtrees drops this to O(n).

algorithms.name: Tower of Hanoi
algorithms.tagline: Solve n-1, move one disk, solve n-1 again.
explanation: The recursive insight: to move n disks from A to C, first move the top n-1 disks out of the way onto B, move the biggest disk to C, then move those n-1 disks from B onto C.

The recurrence T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + 1 gives exactly 2ⁿ − 1 moves, which is provably optimal. It is the cleanest demonstration that a problem can be trivial to describe recursively and hopeless iteratively.
algorithms.example:
3 disks, A -> C
1: disk 1 A->C
2: disk 2 A->B
3: disk 1 C->B
4: disk 3 A->C
5: disk 1 B->A
6: disk 2 B->C
7: disk 1 A->C

frames.note: Move 3 disks from A to C using B as a spare (smaller disks sit on top).
Move 1: disk 1 from A to C.
Move 2: disk 2 from A to B.
Move 3: disk 1 from C to B.
Move 4: disk 3 from A to C.
Move 5: disk 1 from B to A.
Move 6: disk 2 from B to C.
Move 7: disk 1 from A to C.
Solved in 7 moves — the minimum for 3 disks is 2³ − 1 = 7.

title: Divide & Conquer
blurb: Split, solve, combine — with the recurrences that explain the running times.

algorithms.name: Merge Sort as Divide & Conquer
algorithms.tagline: Split, solve, combine — the canonical recurrence.
explanation: Divide and conquer has three steps: divide the input into independent pieces, conquer each recursively, and combine the results. Merge sort divides in O(1), conquers two halves, and combines in O(n).
That gives T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n), which the Master Theorem resolves to O(n log n). The log n comes from the depth of splitting, and the n from the merging done at each level.

frames.note: Divide and conquer: split until each piece is trivially sorted, then merge upwards.
Compare 38 and 27 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 43 and 3 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 27 and 3 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 27 and 43 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 38 and 43 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 9 and 82 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 9 and 10 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 82 and 10 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 3 and 9 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 27 and 9 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 27 and 10 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 27 and 82 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 38 and 82 — the smaller one goes out first.
Compare 43 and 82 — the smaller one goes out first.
Each level does O(n) merging work and there are log n levels — O(n log n).

algorithms.name: Binary Search (recurrence view)
explanation: Binary search is divide and conquer where one of the two halves is thrown away instead of solved. There is no combine step, so the recurrence is T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) and the answer is O(log n).
The recursive form uses O(log n) stack space; the iterative form is O(1). Both need a sorted input — that precondition is where most bugs come from.
algorithms.example:
[2,5,8,12,16,23,38,56,72,91], target 23
lo=0 hi=9 mid=4 -> 16 < 23, go right
lo=5 hi=9 mid=7 -> 56 > 23, go left
lo=5 hi=6 mid=5 -> 23 found at index 5

frames.note: Search for 23 by halving the problem each step.
16 < 23 — discard that half and recurse on [5..9].
56 > 23 — discard that half and recurse on [5..6].
Found 23 at index 5 after 4 halvings at most.

algorithms.name: Maximum Subarray (D&C)
algorithms.tagline: Left, right, or straddling the middle.
explanation: The best subarray either lies entirely in the left half, entirely in the right half, or crosses the midpoint. The first two are recursive calls; the crossing case is a linear scan outwards from the middle.

That linear combine step gives T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n). It is a useful benchmark: Kadane's algorithm solves the same problem in O(n), showing that divide and conquer is not always the best fit.
algorithms.example:
[-2, 5, -1, 7, -6, 3, 4]
left half best: 5 + (-1) = 4
right half best: 3 + 4 = 7
crossing: 5 + (-1) + 7 = 11
Answer: 11

frames.note: Maximum subarray by divide and conquer: best-left, best-right, or a sum that crosses the middle.
Single element base case at index 0: -2.
Single element base case at index 1: 5.
Single element base case at index 2: -1.
Single element base case at index 3: 7.
Single element base case at index 4: -6.
Single element base case at index 5: 3.
Single element base case at index 6: 4.
Maximum subarray sum is 12 (5, −1, 7). Kadane solves the same thing in O(n).

title: Backtracking
blurb: Choose, explore, un-choose — N-Queens, power sets and maze solving.

algorithms.name: N-Queens
algorithms.tagline: Place, recurse, and undo when it fails.
explanation: Backtracking is brute force with early exits. Queens are placed one row at a time; before placing, we check the column and both diagonals. An attacked square is rejected without ever exploring the millions of boards below it.
When a row has no safe square, the algorithm undoes the previous placement and tries the next column — the 'un-choose' step is what makes it backtracking rather than plain recursion.
algorithms.example:
4x4 board
row 0: col 0 -> row 1: cols 0,1 attacked, col 2 ok
row 2: every column attacked -> backtrack
row 0: col 1 -> row 1: col 3 -> row 2: col 0 -> row 3: col 2
Solution: (0,1) (1,3) (2,0) (3,2)

frames.note: 4-Queens: place one queen per row so none attack each other.
Place a queen at (0, 0) and recurse into row 1.
Row 1, column 0 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 1, column 1 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Place a queen at (1, 2) and recurse into row 2.
Row 2, column 0 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 2, column 1 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 2, column 2 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 2, column 3 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Dead end below (1, 2) — undo the move and try the next column.
Place a queen at (1, 3) and recurse into row 2.
Row 2, column 0 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Place a queen at (2, 1) and recurse into row 3.
Row 3, column 0 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 3, column 1 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 3, column 2 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 3, column 3 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Dead end below (2, 1) — undo the move and try the next column.
Row 2, column 2 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 2, column 3 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Dead end below (1, 3) — undo the move and try the next column.
Dead end below (0, 0) — undo the move and try the next column.
Place a queen at (0, 1) and recurse into row 1.
Row 1, column 0 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 1, column 1 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 1, column 2 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Place a queen at (1, 3) and recurse into row 2.
Place a queen at (2, 0) and recurse into row 3.
Row 3, column 0 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Row 3, column 1 is attacked — prune this branch immediately.
Place a queen at (3, 2) and recurse into row 4.
Solution found: every row, column and diagonal holds at most one queen.

algorithms.name: Subsets / Power Set
algorithms.tagline: Include it or skip it, all the way down.
explanation: Every element gets a binary decision: in the subset or not. The recursion tree therefore has 2ⁿ leaves, and each leaf is one subset.
The template — choose, recurse, un-choose — is the same one used for permutations, combinations and combination-sum. Sorting the input first lets you skip duplicates cleanly.

frames.note: Generate every subset by deciding include / exclude for each element.

algorithms.name: Rat in a Maze
algorithms.tagline: Explore a path, retreat at dead ends.
explanation: From each open cell the rat tries the four directions in a fixed order. Walls, out-of-bounds cells and cells already on the current path are rejected, which prevents loops.
If every direction fails, the cell is popped off the path — literally retracing its steps. The same skeleton solves word search, flood fill and Sudoku.
algorithms.example:
Maze (# = wall)
. # # #
. . # #
# . # #
. . . .
down, down blocked -> right, down, down, right, right -> exit (3,3)

frames.note: Rat in a maze: # is a wall. Find a path from the top-left to the bottom-right.
Path found; the highlighted cells are the route.

title: Dynamic Programming
blurb: Tables filling in front of you: Fibonacci, knapsack, LCS and coin change.

algorithms.name: Fibonacci: Memo vs Tabulation
algorithms.tagline: The gateway drug of dynamic programming.
explanation: DP applies when a problem has optimal substructure (the answer is built from answers to smaller versions) and overlapping subproblems (those smaller versions repeat).

Top-down memoisation keeps the recursion and adds a cache. Bottom-up tabulation fills an array from the base cases upwards, which avoids stack depth entirely. Fibonacci only needs the last two cells, so space collapses to O(1).
algorithms.example:
dp[0]=0, dp[1]=1
dp[2]=1, dp[3]=2, dp[4]=3, dp[5]=5
dp[6]=8, dp[7]=13, dp[8]=21, dp[9]=34
9 additions instead of 2⁹ recursive calls.

frames.note: Bottom-up table for Fibonacci — no recursion, no repeated work.
Seed the base cases fib(0) = 0 and fib(1) = 1.
Each cell was filled exactly once — O(n) time, and O(1) space if you keep only the last two values.

algorithms.name: 0/1 Knapsack
algorithms.tagline: Take it or leave it, maximise the value.
explanation: Each item is either in the bag or not. dp[i][w] is the best value using the first i items with capacity w, and it equals max(skip the item, take the item + best value for the remaining capacity).

It is pseudo-polynomial: the cost depends on the numeric capacity W, not just on the item count. Rolling the table down to a single row reduces space to O(W) — iterate w downwards so each item is used once.
algorithms.example:
items (w,v): (1,1) (3,4) (4,5) (5,7), capacity 7
best with 1st two items at w=7: 5
add (4,5): 4+1 -> value 9 at w=7
add (5,7): 7+1 = 8 < 9
Answer 9 (items 2 and 3).

frames.note: 0/1 knapsack, capacity 7. Row i = first i items, column w = capacity w.
Item 1 weighs 1 > 0 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (0).
Item 2 weighs 3 > 0 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (0).
Item 2 weighs 3 > 1 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (1).
Item 2 weighs 3 > 2 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (1).
Item 3 weighs 4 > 0 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (0).
Item 3 weighs 4 > 1 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (1).
Item 3 weighs 4 > 2 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (1).
Item 3 weighs 4 > 3 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (4).
Item 4 weighs 5 > 0 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (0).
Item 4 weighs 5 > 1 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (1).
Item 4 weighs 5 > 2 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (1).
Item 4 weighs 5 > 3 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (4).
Item 4 weighs 5 > 4 — it cannot fit, copy the value above (5).
The bottom-right cell holds the answer: maximum value 9.

algorithms.name: Longest Common Subsequence
algorithms.tagline: The engine behind diff tools.
explanation: Compare the last characters of the two prefixes. If they match, the LCS grows by one on top of the diagonal cell. If not, the answer is the better of dropping one character from either string.
The filled table also encodes the alignment: walking backwards from the bottom-right reconstructs the subsequence, which is exactly what git diff and edit-distance tools do.
algorithms.example:
A = "ABCBDAB", B = "BDCAB"
LCS length = 4
One valid subsequence: "BCAB"
(characters in order, not necessarily contiguous)

frames.note: LCS length is 4 (e.g. "BCAB"). Walk backwards through the table to recover the string itself.

algorithms.name: Coin Change (min coins)
algorithms.tagline: Where greedy fails and DP wins.
explanation: dp[x] is the fewest coins that make amount x. For each amount, try every coin: using that coin costs one coin plus dp[x - coin]. Take the minimum.
Greedy (always take the biggest coin) is wrong for coin systems like {1, 3, 4}: for 6 it gives 4+1+1 = 3 coins while the optimum is 3+3 = 2. DP checks all options, so it is correct for any coin set.
algorithms.example:
coins {1, 3, 4}, target 6
dp: [0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2]
dp[6] = 2  (3 + 3)
Greedy would answer 3 (4 + 1 + 1).

frames.note: Minimum coins to make each amount up to 6 using {1, 3, 4}.

title: Greedy Algorithms
blurb: Locally optimal choices — scheduling, coins and fractional knapsack, plus when greedy breaks.

algorithms.name: Activity Selection
algorithms.tagline: Always pick the meeting that ends first.
explanation: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice and never reconsiders. Here the choice is: among the activities that still fit, take the one that finishes earliest, because it leaves the most room for everything else.
An exchange argument proves it optimal — any optimal schedule can be rewritten to start with the earliest-finishing activity without losing anything. Sorting dominates the cost at O(n log n).

frames.note: Sort activities by finishing time — the greedy choice is always the one that frees the room earliest.
Starts at 1 ≥ last finish — take it. Room is now busy until 4.
Starts at 5 ≥ last finish — take it. Room is now busy until 7.
Starts at 8 ≥ last finish — take it. Room is now busy until 11.
3 activities fit, and no other schedule can beat that.

algorithms.name: Greedy Coin Change
algorithms.tagline: Fast and correct — for canonical coin systems.
explanation: Repeatedly take the largest coin that does not overshoot. For canonical systems such as {1, 5, 10, 25} this provably gives the fewest coins.
It is a great illustration of greedy's limitation: change {1, 3, 4} for 6 and greedy answers three coins while DP finds two. Always check whether your coin system is canonical before trusting greedy.

frames.note: Make 63¢ with US coins, always grabbing the largest coin that fits.
25¢ no longer fits into 13¢ — move to the next denomination.
10¢ no longer fits into 3¢ — move to the next denomination.
5¢ no longer fits into 3¢ — move to the next denomination.
1¢ no longer fits into 0¢ — move to the next denomination.
6 coins. This greedy rule is optimal for {1,5,10,25} but not for arbitrary coin sets.

algorithms.name: Fractional Knapsack
algorithms.tagline: Value density beats brute force.
explanation: When items can be split, sorting by value/weight and filling greedily is optimal — every unit of capacity is spent on the most valuable material available.
Contrast this with 0/1 knapsack, where the all-or-nothing constraint breaks the greedy argument and forces dynamic programming. One small rule change flips the right technique.
algorithms.example:
items (w,v): (10,60) (20,100) (30,120), capacity 50
ratios: 6, 5, 4
take 10 -> value 60, cap 40
take 20 -> value 160, cap 20
take 20/30 of the last -> +80
Total 240.

frames.note: Sort by value-per-unit-weight — the greedy order for the fractional version.
Whole item fits: +60 value, 40 capacity left.
Whole item fits: +100 value, 20 capacity left.
Only 20 units fit — take the fraction for +80 value.
Maximum value 240. Fractions make greedy optimal; the 0/1 version needs DP.

title: Bit Manipulation
blurb: Masks, shifts and XOR identities that replace loops and extra memory with single instructions.

algorithms.name: Get, Set, Clear, Toggle
algorithms.tagline: The four masks every bit trick is built from.
explanation: A single integer can hold a whole set of flags. Shifting 1 left by k builds a mask that isolates bit k, and AND, OR, XOR and NOT then read or edit that bit in one CPU instruction.

Read: (n >> k) & 1. Set: n | (1 << k). Clear: n & ~(1 << k). Toggle: n ^ (1 << k). Shifting left multiplies by two, shifting right divides — use >>> for unsigned right shifts in JavaScript, since bitwise operators work on 32-bit signed integers.

frames.note: Start with n = 44 — binary 00101100 (bit 0 is on the right).
Left shift by 1 doubles the value: 10 << 1 = 20.

algorithms.name: Count Set Bits
algorithms.tagline: n & (n - 1) erases the lowest 1 each pass.
explanation: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and turns every zero below it into a 1. ANDing with the original therefore removes exactly that one bit and leaves the rest untouched.
Brian Kernighan's loop runs once per set bit instead of once per bit of width, which matters for sparse masks. The related idiom n & -n isolates the lowest set bit rather than clearing it.

frames.note: Brian Kernighan's trick: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit.
n & (n - 1) removed it. Set bits counted so far: 1.
n & (n - 1) removed it. Set bits counted so far: 2.
n & (n - 1) removed it. Set bits counted so far: 3.
n & (n - 1) removed it. Set bits counted so far: 4.
The loop runs once per set bit, not once per bit width.

algorithms.name: Single Number (XOR)
algorithms.tagline: Pairs cancel; the loner remains.
explanation: XOR has three properties that make this work: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and it is commutative and associative. XOR-ing the whole array in any order therefore cancels every duplicated pair.
A hash map solves the same problem in O(n) memory; XOR does it with a single integer. The same idea finds a missing number in 0..n by XOR-ing indices with values.

frames.note: Every value appears twice except one. XOR cancels the pairs.
a ^ a = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so the pairs vanish and only 4 survives — O(n) time, O(1) space.
